source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: Eleven LLMs played Wason's 2-4-6 rule-discovery game (propose a triple, get yes/no, guess the rule). They mostly proposed tests their current guess predicted. Success was low and varied widely. Models that tested more outside their guess (higher incompatible-to-compatible ratio, I:C) succeeded more. Thinking mode raised success but not consistently I:C, so thinking gains were not simply less confirmation.
numbers: 45-turn cap; 80 test episodes per model-variant (5 triples x 4 rule sets x 4 target rules); success from 6% to 78% across models. Baseline thinking models: Qwen3-8B 21%, 14B 34%, 32B 41%, QwQ-32B 50%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 73%; non-thinking: Qwen3-8B 6%, 14B 23%, 32B 33%, Llama-3.3-70B 21%, GPT-4o 11%. I:C 0.14-0.66 for thinking baselines. Positive success-vs-I:C correlation in both groups. Human reference in paper: 6/29 right on first announcement, I:C 1.79 vs 0.24.
quote: LLMs exhibit confirmation bias, often proposing triples to confirm their hypothesis rather than trying to falsify it.
limits: Synthetic integer-triple rules, 4 test rule sets with one human-derived rule each; LLM-as-judge for rule match; correlation not causation; model set mostly Qwen3 plus a few others; preprint, one author group.
agent_relevance: Gap 6/7. Supports a code check at the S7 step: log whether the next test is compatible with the current guess and force one incompatible test when the ratio is low. Fits K03 and K18.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, interventions section (Think-in-Opposites, Dual-Goal)
finding: A prompt-only negative-test instruction (Think-in-Opposites, TiO: pick one feature of the last test and test its opposite) raised success in every model-mode pair. Dual-Goal (name the rule and its complement) helped thinking models but hurt several non-thinking ones. Gains were significant for thinking models; for non-thinking models I:C did not change significantly. TiO also raised tokens per turn for thinking models, so it is not an equal-token comparison.
numbers: Abstract: rule discovery 42% to 56% on average. Thinking: Qwen3-8B 21% to 36% (TiO); Qwen3-32B 41% to 61% (TiO); Gemini-2.5-Pro 73% to 78% under both TiO and Dual-Goal (per-model Dual-Goal numbers for the small Qwen thinking runs were garbled in text extraction and are not quoted). Non-thinking Qwen3-14B Dual-Goal 23% to 13%; Qwen3-32B Dual-Goal 33% to 10%; GPT-4o TiO 11% to 16%. Tokens per turn thinking Qwen3-8B 1088 baseline vs 1716 TiO vs 2143 Dual-Goal. Dual-Goal improved success in 8 of 11 model-mode cells, TiO in all 11; I:C rose in 18 of 22 cases.
quote: Think-in-Opposites improves task success in all.
limits: No equal-token control: thinking models spent 20-100% more tokens per turn under the interventions. One prompt wording per intervention. Only numeric triples plus one transfer task.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 answer: the instruction survives on thinking modes and mostly on non-thinking ones (small gains), but Dual-Goal is risky on weak or non-thinking models. Use TiO-style wording, not Dual-Goal, and measure tokens.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify, Blicket transfer and distillation
finding: Outside numeric triples, in the Blicket detector task, TiO prompting helped thinking models clearly but gave mixed or negative results for some non-thinking models. Models fine-tuned on TiO behaviour from the Wason task transferred part of the gain to Blicket without a prompt, but less than a TiO prompt in Blicket itself.
numbers: Blicket: 192 episodes per model (4 or 8 objects x 2 or 3 blickets x AND/OR/XOR x 16). Thinking Qwen3-8B 32% to 40% (TiO), Qwen3-32B 57% to 86%, QwQ-32B 80% to 82%. Non-thinking: Qwen3-14B 25% to 20%, Qwen3-32B 64% to 56%, Llama-3.3-70B 78% to 82%. Distilled-from-Wason Qwen3-32B+32B TiO 77% (base 57%, prompted TiO 86%); Qwen3-8B variants 34-38% (base 32%, prompted 40%). Wason distillation: Qwen3-8B 21% to 36%; cross-scale+TiO (8B student, 32B teacher) 59%.
quote: falsification-oriented exploration learned in the Wason task transfers to a new domain
limits: Blicket hypotheses have no clear opposite, so Dual-Goal was not run. Distillation needs training, which our agent does not do.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 transfer: a negative-test instruction does move behaviour outside number triples on thinking modes; on non-thinking modes it can lose. Test per mode before putting it in S7.

source: Chari and Pattanaik (2026) Wild Guesses and Mild Guesses in Active Concept Learning
finding: A learner whose hypotheses are Python programs proposed by Gemini 2.5 Flash chose queries by approximate expected information gain (EIG), by a positive test strategy (PTS: query what the best guess says is positive), or at random. EIG was not better on simple rules, and was better on compound rules where falsification is needed. The authors name a support-mismatch trap: highly diagnostic boundary queries push the posterior to regions where the LLM proposes invalid or overly specific programs. On hard rules most methods failed.
numbers: Number Game, X={0..100}, budget 50 queries, convergence at 0.95 mass on MAP (queries to converge, EIG / PTS / random). Easy: squares 3/2/2; multiples of 4: 7/4/2; odd: 8/6/5; powers of 2: 5/2/2. Medium: even <30: 17/31/17; multiples of 3 or 7: 8/DNF/13; odd multiples of 3: 14/35/21; ending in 6: 4/7/7. Hard: digits sum<8: 43/DNF/DNF; remainder 5 mod 9: 31/DNF/41; the other two hard rules DNF for all.
quote: EIG is effective when falsification is necessary (e.g., compound or exception-laden rules), but underperforms on simple concepts.
limits: Workshop paper, apparently one run per cell (no variance), one proposal model, about 12 rules, number-game domain only. Tokens or calls not compared (EIG needs the particle set).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 answer in part: code-side EIG on model-generated hypotheses is not a free win. It beats random and PTS on compound rules but loses on simple ones because it drives the model out of its own proposal support. Suggests a switch rule: cheap confirm-style tests first, EIG-like tests when progress stalls (the paper's meta-policy idea, untested).

source: From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context? (2026), BED-LLM versus naive in-context EIG
finding: The authors re-ran BED-LLM (code does the belief and information-gain arithmetic; the LLM only gives single likelihoods) against a naive baseline in which a reasoning model is told in one prompt to list up to 10 candidate animals, score 10 questions by expected information gain and ask the best. With three current open reasoning models the naive baseline matched BED-LLM across the game and exceeded it in parts. So the harness benefit seen on 2024-era models did not hold for current reasoning models on 20 Questions.
numbers: 20Q, 40 target animals, T=20 questions, temperature 1.0, three open reasoning models; accuracy-by-iteration figure only (no table of numbers read). Separate result: non-reasoning models show a posterior-mass gap to the active oracle of at least 30% on 20Q and ProteinWorld-simple.
quote: the naive baseline matches BED-LLM across the discovery process and exceeds it in parts.
limits: Guessing game with a closed hypothesis list; exact numbers are in a figure; open-weight models only; the baseline prompt itself contains the whole EIG procedure, so it is a scaffold, not a plain prompt.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: on equal-ish tokens a one-shot in-context EIG recipe in a reasoning mode may be enough, so a code-side pick is justified mainly for non-reasoning models or for auditability. Matches the moving-target warning for harnesses.

source: From Prompts to Posteriors (2026), coherence and posterior fidelity results
finding: Elicited probabilities were incoherent when asked in separate chats and much less so inside one dialogue. Without reasoning, posteriors drifted from the Bayes oracle after a few pieces of evidence even when the ranking was right. Reasoning mode reproduced closed-form posteriors almost exactly; when the likelihood needed Monte Carlo, only reasoning plus code execution matched the oracle.
numbers: Dutch-book tests: ForecastBench questions, 30 scenarios per model-constraint, 3 models. Cross-conversation violation rates above 50% for almost all cells; within-dialogue about 10% (Gemini-2.5-Pro) and 1 of 30 (Gemma). ProteinWorld main setting 5 worlds x 8 classes x 8 attributes x 6 experiments (40 runs). Example: no reasoning gave 0.643/0.357 vs oracle 0.967/0.033; reasoning gave 0.967/0.033. Hard ProteinWorld: Gemini-2.5-Pro reasoning alone high KL, with code execution KL near 0.
quote: LLMs generally violate Bayes' rule in context, but that reasoning and code execution substantially improve performance.
limits: Synthetic worlds with stated likelihoods, so this tests the arithmetic of updating, not whether the model can supply sound P(E|H) for real analytic evidence. Exact numbers are mostly in figures.
agent_relevance: Gap 5/8. Updating arithmetic should live in code or in a reasoning pass; ask for conditional likelihoods inside one dialogue, not in isolated calls, and sum-check in code (G4/G5).

source: Ling (2026) From Hindsight to Foresight: Dissecting Clinical Evidence Acquisition in LLMs, evidence-value decomposition
finding: After matching the number of facts, the remaining foresight deficit is mostly which facts were obtained, not how they were read or ordered. Swapping the foresight fact set for the hindsight-selected set gave the biggest jump; reordering the same set gave a smaller one; reversing the hindsight order cost about as much as swapping sets, so order matters too. Few of the facts the retrospective selector ranked top were ever requested.
numbers: Primary cohort N=181. k=3: foresight 33.1% vs count-matched hindsight 63.0% (gap 29.8 points, CI 22.1-37.6); k=6: 42.0% vs 70.7% (gap 28.7); continuation k=12 gap 21.4. Critical Evidence Recall 16.0% at k=3 and 35.7% at k=12; hindsight Top-1 fact never reached within six requests in 64.6% of cases. Panel C (N=100, normalized six-prefix accuracy): reranking the foresight set 34.3% to 43.7% (+9.3); set replacement 43.7% to 70.3% (+26.7); reversing hindsight order 70.3% to 44.3% (-26.0).
quote: Evidence identity and order therefore make distinct contributions
limits: Hindsight reference facts are chosen by an LLM selector that sees the realized case, so critical is model-defined, not clinician-defined. Single preprint under review; case-level breakdown by category is in figures only. Same model family judges and acts.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 answer: the gap is mainly choice of facts (about 27 of 30 points when sets are swapped), plus order (about 26 when hindsight is reversed). For S7: the weak step is picking what to ask, so code should score candidate requests by how much they separate hypotheses, not just collect more.

source: Ling (2026) Hindsight to Foresight, request failures and recovery
finding: Many evidence requests produce nothing new, and recovery after a failed request is only partial. After a duplicate, switching request category worked much better than staying; after a no-match the pattern reversed. A fixed menu of candidate targets (result-blind) did not beat free-form requests, so the problem is not text matching.
numbers: Of request slots: 58.7% new unique fact, 25.3% repeat, 16.0% no match; three requests give 2.09 unique facts. Menu and free-form foresight both 31.7% at k=3 vs hindsight 75.0%. Next request gets new evidence after 83/194 duplicates (42.8%) and 51/149 no-match (34.2%). After duplicate: switch category 49.7% vs stay 17.1%; after no-match: switch 27.6% vs stay 65.4%.
quote: Only 58.7% of request slots yield a new unique fact
limits: Recovery rates are associations, not interventions: no test of a hard block on repeats. Clinical case vignettes with a canonical fact store; the matcher can mis-map requests.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: duplicates and no-matches are about 41% of requests. A code block on repeats is cheap and sensible, but the data do not show it helps; the better-supported lever is forcing a change of category after a duplicate.

source: Ling (2026) Hindsight to Foresight, controlled rescue
finding: Adding one unseen high-ranked fact to an incorrect foresight state rescued many diagnoses, more than adding a matched control fact; the effect scaled with the fact's rank and did not clearly depend on when it was added. This is direct evidence that one decisive item among many is missed and that supplying it changes the answer.
numbers: Prespecified complete-grid cohort: critical-minus-control rescue +38.8 points for hindsight Rank 1, +24.8 Rank 2, +10.3 Rank 3; Rank1-minus-Rank3 +28.5. Insertion at k=1 vs k=12 for Rank 1 not clearly different. Positive in all 15 rank-by-depth cells in the all-eligible analysis. JSD 0.633 hindsight vs 0.531 foresight, but reference-diagnosis probability gain 0.298 vs 0.084 at k=3.
quote: omission of high-value evidence can directly contribute to diagnostic failure
limits: Rank is defined by an LLM selector with hindsight; the rescue is measured in the same model family. Update size (JSD) did not track truth-directed gain.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (indirect): supports a step that surfaces the single most discriminating item for explicit weighing. Warns that a big change in the distribution is not a signal that evidence was used well.

source: Wu (2026) Split the Labor: Separating Evidence Interpretation from Decision Aggregation
finding: Design paper: have the model read each source alone and emit a fixed tuple (hypothesis, reliability bucket, rationale, provenance); combine in code by pooling calibrated log-likelihood ratios. It shows analytically that summing unnormalised vote weights drifts with source count (count-scale drift) and that LLR pooling fixes it. Reliability buckets are built from observable properties of the reading (source length, grounded rationale), not from elicited confidence, because elicited confidence is poorly calibrated.
numbers: Medical longitudinal corpus; the survival-model instantiation reaches AUPRC 0.921 vs 0.805 for a hand-crafted baseline (a different part of the paper). The LLR pooling itself is derived, not deployed; the measured system uses a weighted vote.
quote: We do not use elicited model confidence, since it is poorly calibrated.
limits: Not an ACH test and not a test of LLM-supplied likelihood ratios; domain is clinical records; empirical claims concern the partition, not the LLR rule; single-author preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 1/5: the architecture matches per-item rating in the model, aggregation in code. It does not show that the model's per-item likelihood ratios are good. Keep it as a design pattern, not evidence.

source: Bayesian Coherence Coefficient study (2025) Are LLM Belief Updates Consistent with Bayes' Theorem? (ICML 2025 workshop)
finding: Pre-trained (base) models were given evidence texts and the shift in the probability of one class versus another was compared with the shift expected from the model's own conditional likelihoods. The correlation (BCC) was positive for all models and rose with size. But the slope was well below 1: models under-update relative to their own likelihoods.
numbers: 6,460 (class pair, evidence, history) instances per model; 10 categories, at least 5 classes and 20 evidence texts each. BCC vs log parameter count r=0.906, p<1e-6. Update gradient 0.295 (Falcon3 1.7B) to 0.482 (Qwen2.5 14.8B); direction agreement 63.7% (Pythia 0.2B) to 75.8%. Benchmarks BBH, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, MATH L5 positive (p<0.01).
quote: larger and more capable models are more coherent with Bayes' theorem
limits: Small base models only (largest 14.8B); dataset generated by GPT-4o; the expected update comes from the model itself, so it measures self-consistency, not accuracy of P(E|H). Table values read from a page summary of the HTML version, not the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: model-internal likelihoods are directionally right about 3 times in 4 but update too little. Do not trust raw verbalised updates; compute the update in code from rated likelihoods.

source: Samanta et al. (2026) BayesBench: Evaluating LLM Belief Trajectories Under Multi-Turn Evidence Accumulation
finding: Seven open-weight LLMs (3B-70B) updated beliefs over turns in bookbag-and-poker-chip style tasks. Scale improved latent inference, but gains did not carry to downstream prediction; larger models over-updated toward extremes in the coin task and pushed middle triage labels to extremes. Active engagement with a simulated user produced a persistent pro-user bias compared with passively reading the same evidence.
numbers: Four environments (coin flip, recommender, social judgment, medical triage); closed-form Bayes reference only for two. Exact per-model numbers are in figures and were not read.
quote: a persistent pro-user bias relative to passive observation of the same evidence
limits: Open-weight models up to 70B; many numbers only in figures; preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: a measured case where talking to a user who holds a stance shifts the model beyond the evidence, which disappears under passive reading of the same evidence. Supports a read-evidence-without-the-user's-hypothesis step, but not tested as a fix on evidence search.

source: He, Qiu, Sap, Shirado (2025) Martingale Score: An Unsupervised Metric for Bayesian Rationality in LLM Reasoning
finding: Under rational updating, future beliefs should not be predictable from the current belief. In forecasting, value-laden questions and paper review, LLM belief updates were predictable from the prior (belief entrenchment) across models, reasoning styles and system prompts. A critical-thinking system prompt reduced it in forecasting and a prior-conforming prompt increased it. Higher entrenchment tracked worse forecast accuracy.
numbers: Martingale scores (95% CI) with chain of thought: ChangeMyView 0.103 +/- 0.013, Forecasting 0.037 +/- 0.011, OpenReview 0.086 +/- 0.012. At a score of about 0.04 forecasting performance was worse than random guessing; 0.0 would be calibrated.
quote: future beliefs are consistently predictable from the model's current belief
limits: Open-ended domains with noisy labels; link to accuracy is correlational except in forecasting where the authors run a causal check; belief is an elicited number.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: an agent that has stated a leading hypothesis tends to hold it. Supports running the S7 test under a neutral restatement of all hypotheses and logging belief drift as a check.

source: Zou and Xu (2026) WORTH Benchmark: Evidence Discovery under Not-Fully-Cooperative Information (two-episode pilot)
finding: Models read unmarked mystery stories, chose key clue sentences and named participants. Finding clues did not predict naming the right people. In Episode 2 almost all runs converged on the same wrong set, and models chose suspicion-oriented sentences but never the adjacent exoneration-oriented ones. This is a case of a decisive exculpatory item among many not being used.
numbers: 70 runs, 67 scorable. Ep.1: 120 sentences, 12 key clues, 6 models x 5 runs, mean key-clue hits 2.2-3.4 of 12; GPT-5.6 Sol most clues (3.4) but fewest correct people (0.8 of 3), DeepSeek-V4-Flash fewest clues (2.2) and best people (1.6, zero wrong). Ep.2: 134 sentences, 20 key clues, 37 scorable runs; 31/37 (83.8%) chose the same trio, 16/37 (43.2%) exactly that trio; suspicion sentences chosen 25 times, exoneration sentences 0 times. Gemini 3.1 Pro scored 6 or 19 with confidence 100 every run.
quote: adjacent suspicion-oriented and exoneration-oriented sentences were selected 25 times and 0 times, respectively.
limits: Authors say pilot only: two stories authored by the benchmark team, no stable ranking, human data not reported; clue scoring is author-defined.
agent_relevance: Gap 1/3: shows the failure a discriminating-evidence step should catch: confirming-looking items get chosen, exculpatory ones do not. A plain-model baseline here is itself weak; forced ACH-style scoring of each sentence against all suspects is the obvious test, not yet run.

source: Kern and Doherty (1982) 'Pseudodiagnosticity' in an idealized medical problem-solving environment, J Med Educ 57(2):100-104
finding: Sixty-five senior medical students chose which symptom information would help judge between two diagnoses. Most chose information about the hypothesis they already had, rather than the matching figure under the rival.
numbers: N=65 senior medical students; 83% chose information that Bayes would not require for the comparison (same-hypothesis pseudodiagnostic choices).
limits: Abstract read via the Europe PMC record only; full text not read, so per-item breakdown, wording and other conditions are unknown. Hypothetical vignettes with stated percentages.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: fills a number for K02 (83% for medical students on an idealised task), far from the 30-31% correct figures in another family; task wording matters. Run the same item set on the agent.

source: Wolf, Gruppen, Billi (1988) Use of the competing-hypotheses heuristic to reduce 'pseudodiagnosticity', J Med Educ 63(7):548-554
finding: A brief teaching intervention (competing-hypotheses heuristic plus Bayes' theorem) improved how medical students chose diagnostic data compared with a control group that began equal.
numbers: Quasi-experiment with nonequivalent control group; intervention n=119, control n=89; similar at baseline; after training the intervention group was better, p<.001. Effect size and item-level percentages not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract read via Europe PMC only; nonequivalent groups; no delayed retention test seen; effect size unknown.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a short instruction to name the competing hypothesis and the likelihood under it is teachable to people with p<.001 improvement. It is the human precedent for an S7 prompt line, but no LLM test exists.

source: Anderson and Doherty (2024) Pseudodiagnosticity and preference hierarchy in a search-only inference paradigm, Memory and Cognition 52:826-839
finding: People still pick same-hypothesis cues when they cannot see any percentages, so the bias is in the search, not only in how stated percentages are used. This answers part of the norm-misapplication argument.
numbers: Abstract only: confirmed same-hypothesis pseudodiagnosticity for primary and secondary preferences in a search-only paradigm. No N in the record read.
limits: Abstract read via Europe PMC; no sample size or percentages seen.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: K02 should stay contested on size but not on existence: the bias appears even without numbers. Test the agent with no-number items to separate search habit from percentage reading.

source: Crupi and Girotto (2014) From is to ought, and back: how normative concerns foster progress in reasoning research, Front Psychol
finding: Review of how normative analysis changed reasoning research. For pseudodiagnosticity it states the simplest task (given Pr(e|h)=65%, pick one of Pr(e|not h), Pr(f|h), Pr(f|not h)), reports that Crupi et al. (2009) recast the standard answer as norm misapplication, that Tweney et al. (2010) disputed this, and says the classical interpretation is now judged inadequate by all parties.
numbers: No participant percentages in the article.
limits: Secondary review, no data. It confirms the dispute, not its size.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: confirms why K02 stays contested; the Doherty 1979 choice percentages remain unobtained.

source: Related-work claims in Prompts to Posteriors (2026): Kossen et al. 2024, Falck et al. 2024, Chlon et al. 2026 on in-context Bayes
finding: The paper states that general-purpose LLMs violate exchangeability, weight evidence by its position in context, and are Bayesian only in expectation over context orderings. These are second-hand statements; the cited papers were not opened.
numbers: No numbers given in the passage.
quote: weight evidence by its position in context
limits: Second-hand; relevant to evidence order but not to row versus column hypothesis-table layout.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: suggests shuffling evidence order and averaging across orders for the S7 rating step. No LLM study of rows-vs-columns hypothesis tables was found in this pass.
